# What's new in Nucleo


### A brief overview of recent company and product updates from the Nucleo team.


[Angelica Iacovelli](https://substack.com/@angelicaiacovelli)


,[Tisha Mazumdar](https://substack.com/@tishamazumdarnucleo)


, and[Luca Pegolotti](https://substack.com/@lucapegolotti)


Sep 09, 2026


Two updates this month: a pilot taking shape with Northwestern Medicine, and body composition reports generated automatically from MRI.


## Northwestern Medicine: structuring a pilot together


Northwestern Medicine is one of the largest academic health systems in the United States, with 11 hospitals and more than 5,400 affiliated physicians. In July they invested in Nucleo. In August we spent a week on site with their clinical teams in Chicago, and we are now structuring a pilot together.


> *A week on site with the Northwestern Medicine team in Chicago.*


## Body composition from MRI


Nucleo’s Body composition has so far been a CT product. It now runs on MRI, with the report generated automatically from suitable chemical shift encoded water–fat separation (Dixon) or single-echo T1-weighted/T1-like acquisitions. In addition to skeletal muscle, subcutaneous, and visceral adipose tissue, we also report muscle quality and ectopic fat.


*Where Fat Is Stored Matters.* Body composition metrics that collapse the body into total mass, total fat mass or total lean mass can miss where fat is stored and what is happening inside muscle. MRI is useful because it preserves anatomy: when the field of view includes the relevant regions, it can separate subcutaneous from visceral fat and localize fat in and around muscle groups and organs. Dixon adds a second layer: fat-water separation lets those tissues be reported as fat-fraction measurements rather than only as segmentation volumes or intensity-based proxies.


*Tissue classes on MRI.*


*Muscle Quality.* Intramuscular fat is an imaging correlate of myosteatosis: muscle quality can deteriorate even when muscle volume is preserved. On Dixon MRI, this can be measured as fat fraction within segmented muscle regions. On non-Dixon T1-weighted or T1-like scans, the analogous output should be treated as an intensity-based fat proxy. In thigh scans, our current tools also report intramuscular and intermuscular fat across the visible leg musculature.


*Organ and Cardiac Fat* . When the acquisition covers the relevant anatomy, the same MRI can support fat measurements around the heart and in abdominal organs. Epicardial and pericardial fat can be estimated without a dedicated cardiac sequence; epicardial fat is metabolically active and has been associated with cardiovascular and arrhythmic risk. On Dixon acquisitions, hepatic, pancreatic, spleen, and renal fat fraction can also be estimated from the fat-water reconstruction, with hepatic and pancreatic steatosis linked to metabolic risk.


*Thigh inter- and intramuscular fat, epicardial and pericardial fat, and fat fraction in liver, pancreas, spleen and kidneys.*


*Why MRI and not Bioimpedance.* MRI measures body composition from images of the tissues themselves: anatomical compartments are segmented in space, and Dixon acquisitions can add fat-fraction measurements from separated fat and water signals. Bioimpedance is different: it estimates body composition from electrical properties that are strongly influenced by body water. During rapid weight change, especially in the first weeks of an intervention, shifts in hydration and glycogen can move a bioimpedance lean-mass estimate even when true muscle tissue has changed little. MRI is therefore useful when the question is not just whether weight changed, but which tissue compartments changed and where.


With the new MRI capabilities in Nucleo, cohorts that have already been scanned in trials, registries or routine care can be analyzed retrospectively when suitable MRI acquisitions are available and when consent, governance, coverage and image quality support the analysis. If you run a trial with an imaging endpoint, or have a cohort that has already been scanned, we would like to hear from you.
